VBO:0200013.summary: Alanos Españoles are steady, sociable workers historically used to manage cattle and guard rural property. Affectionate toward people and ready to learn, they have a tradition of working in teams with other adult dogs; records of the breed in Iberia reach back to the fourteenth century.
VBO:0200013.shortDescription: A steady Iberian cattle worker, the Alano Español is known for teamwork, ready learning and an affectionate manner.

sources.title: RSCE Alano Español national breed standard
sources.evidence: RSCE standard documents cattle handling, estate guarding, Iberian history from the fourteenth century, teamwork, sociability, learning and affection.

VBO:0200027.summary: American Akitas are alert, responsive dogs with a dignified, courageous character. Their line grew from Japanese Akita stock brought to the United States after World War II and developed separately there; the breed standard also notes that some can react strongly to other dogs, especially of the same sex.
VBO:0200027.shortDescription: Dignified and alert, the American Akita grew from Japanese stock into a distinct US line after World War II.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 344: American Akita
sources.evidence: FCI 344 describes alert, responsive, dignified and courageous temperament, possible same-sex dog reactivity, and US development from postwar Japanese Akita stock.

VBO:0200074.summary: Ariège Pointing Dogs are steady, sociable gundogs known as adaptable hunters and responsive learners. Likely descended from old French pointing dogs, their line gained lighter movement through southern French crosses in the nineteenth century; local hunters kept it alive after wartime decline.
VBO:0200074.shortDescription: Steady and sociable, this Ariège pointer carries an old French hunting line revived by local hunters.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 177: Ariege Pointing Dog
sources.evidence: FCI 177 describes stable sociability toward humans and dogs, docile/trainable character, all-round hunting, French Braque descent and Ariège revival.

VBO:0200132.summary: Vigorous and enterprising on a scent trail, Beagle-Harriers keep a clear, ringing voice and readily join other hounds in a pack. This French breed grew from Beagles, Harriers and local hounds as nineteenth-century hunters sought dogs able to sustain a fast hare chase across changing Gascon terrain.
VBO:0200132.shortDescription: An enterprising French pack hound, the Beagle-Harrier follows scent with stamina and a clear, ringing voice.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 290: Beagle Harrier
sources.evidence: FCI 290 describes the Beagle-Harrier as a balanced, vigorous, agile French scenthound intermediate between Beagle and Harrier; it gives no detailed temperament claims.

sources.title: Société de Vènerie: Le Beagle-Harrier
sources.evidence: French hunting association describes an enterprising, disciplined and tenacious trail worker, clear high-pitched voice, stamina and readiness to join a pack; history credits Baron Gérard’s late-nineteenth-century French development from Beagles, Harriers and local French hounds.

VBO:0200130.summary: Bavarian Mountain Scent Hounds are calm, balanced trackers devoted to their handler and often reserved with strangers. Bred in the nineteenth century from Hanoverian scent hounds and mountain hounds, they follow wounded hoofed game through steep Bavarian terrain with a focused, self-assured working style.
VBO:0200130.shortDescription: Calm and focused, this Bavarian tracker follows difficult mountain trails while staying close to its handler.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 217: Bavarian Mountain Scent Hound
sources.evidence: FCI 217 describes calm balanced temperament, handler devotion, reserve with strangers, wounded-game tracking, and nineteenth-century Hanoverian/mountain-hound origin.

VBO:0200656.summary: Hanoverian Scent Hounds are calm, self-assured trackers that concentrate deeply on a wounded-game trail. Sensitive to their handler and reserved with strangers, they carry a lineage that runs from medieval leash hounds to the hunting estate at Hanover.
VBO:0200656.shortDescription: Calm and intent on a trail, the Hanoverian Scent Hound draws on a long German tracking lineage.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 213: Hanoverian Scent Hound
sources.evidence: FCI 213 describes calm assurance, concentrated tracking, handler sensitivity, discerning reserve and Hanoverian hunting-estate history.

VBO:0200522.summary: Finnish Hounds are calm, friendly dogs with an energetic, independent style on a scent trail. Developed in Finland during the nineteenth century, they traditionally hunt hare and fox and give voice while following a trail; the breed standard records the first written standard in 1932.
VBO:0200522.shortDescription: Friendly and independent on a scent, the Finnish Hound traditionally trails hare and fox with a ringing voice.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 51: Finnish Hound
sources.evidence: FCI 51 describes calm, energetic, friendly temperament; independent hare/fox scent work and vocal trail; nineteenth-century Finnish development and 1932 standard.

VBO:0200537.summary: Gascon Saintongeois hounds are calm, affectionate pack workers with a fine nose and a distinctive carrying voice. The Grand line arose in nineteenth-century southwestern France when the last Saintonge hounds were crossed with Bleu de Gascogne; the Petit was later selected from smaller Grand hounds.
VBO:0200537.shortDescription: Calm and fine-nosed, this southwestern French pack hound is known for a far-carrying voice on the trail.

sources.title: FCI breed standard No. 21: Gascon Saintongeois
sources.evidence: FCI 21 describes calm affectionate amenable pack temperament, fine nose, wide casting and sonorous voice; Grand origin from Saintonge/Bleu de Gascogne, Petit selected later. Artwork depicts a documented Grand as one acknowledged size of the parent breed; this does not claim a separate temperament for either size.

VBO:0201033.summary: Polish Hounds are devoted to their household yet often wary of strangers. On a fresh trail they give tongue loudly as they pursue game, a voice Polish hunters have long treated as part of the chase. This heavier Ogar line once served royal hunts; today its work in Poland centers on wild boar and fox rather than the hares it historically followed.
VBO:0201033.shortDescription: Devoted at home and vocal on a fresh trail, the heavier Polish Ogar once served royal hunts.
VBO:0201033.historicalRoots: Old-established Polish Ogar hound, historically linked to royal hunting and now used for boar and fox.

sources.title: FCI: Polish Hound (Standard No. 52)
sources.evidence: FCI names the Ogar as an old Polish breed, records royal hunts, describes a devoted household dog wary of strangers, giving tongue on the hot trail, and present boar/fox work. It describes a heavier muscular hound with tan head/limbs, dark saddle, hanging ears and low full tail.

sources.title: FCI: Polish Hunting Dog (Standard No. 354)
sources.evidence: Historical summary distinguishes the lighter Polish scent hound/Gończy from the heavier Polish brach/Ogar type.

VBO:0201116.summary: Smooth-faced Pyrenean Sheepdogs are lively and responsive, though some remain wary of strangers. In the Pyrenean foothills, horse dealers and cattle drovers valued this working variety; its separate identity was recognized in the breed standard by the 1920s. The shorter hair around the face makes its quick, attentive expression easy to see.
VBO:0201116.shortDescription: Lively and responsive, this smooth-faced Pyrenean worker was valued by cattle drovers in the foothills.
VBO:0201116.historicalRoots: Smooth-faced Pyrenean sheepdog variety long used in foothill livestock movement; described separately by the 1920s.

sources.title: FCI: Pyrenean Sheepdog – Smooth Faced (Standard No. 138)
sources.evidence: FCI identifies the smooth-faced variety as a lively, biddable sheepdog sometimes wary of strangers, especially valued by horse dealers and cattle drovers in the Pyrenean foothills; a separate standard appendix dates to the 1920s. Short fine facial hair, squarer body and semi-long body coat distinguish it from long-coated relative.

VBO:0201034.summary: Polish Hunting Dogs tend to be steady and gentle, yet courageous on a hunt and watchful around strangers. Their voice changes pitch while following game, a working signal in the forests and difficult southern Polish mountains where they pursued boar and deer. This lithe Gończy type developed separately from the heavier Polish Ogar hound.
VBO:0201034.shortDescription: Steady and gentle, the leaner Polish Gończy gives a changing voice while pursuing game in mountain forests.
VBO:0201034.historicalRoots: Lighter Gończy Polski scent hound retained for boar and deer work in difficult southern Polish mountain terrain.

sources.title: FCI: Polish Hunting Dog (Standard No. 354)
sources.evidence: FCI describes stable gentle temperament, courage, wariness toward strangers and characteristic melodic voice with varied intonation; boar/deer work in southern Polish mountains. Historical section distinguishes lighter Polish scent hound from heavier brach/Ogar type. Medium lithe build, black-and-tan coat and low full tail.

VBO:0200679.summary: Transylvanian Hounds are generally even-tempered and good-natured, while remaining determined and lively on a trail. Once favored for aristocratic hunts, they continued working in the pathless Carpathian woods as agriculture reshaped the region. The long-legged hunting line survived a near disappearance in the twentieth century; its shorter-legged counterpart did not.
VBO:0200679.shortDescription: Even-tempered yet determined on a trail, this Carpathian hound survived near disappearance in the last century.
VBO:0200679.historicalRoots: Long-legged Erdélyi Kopó of Hungarian origin, used for big game in Carpathian woods and rebuilt after near extinction.

sources.title: FCI: Hungarian Hound – Transylvanian Scent Hound (Standard No. 241)
sources.evidence: FCI calls the hound good-natured, courageous, quiet and even but determined and lively. It records aristocratic hunting, retreat to pathless Carpathian woods, long- and short-legged lines, near extinction and breeding resumed in 1968; only long-legged remains. Black coat with tan markings, medium athletic body and full tail.

VBO:0201209.summary: Serbian Tricolor Hounds are devoted and lively companions with the tenacity to keep following a scent. Their independent standing as a breed was settled in 1946, after a period when they were treated as a variety of the Serbian Hound; international recognition followed in 1961.
VBO:0201209.shortDescription: Kind and lively yet persistent on a scent, this Balkan hound was recognized apart from the Serbian Hound.
VBO:0201209.historicalRoots: Balkan tricolored scent hound recognized as distinct from the Serbian Hound in 1946.

sources.title: FCI: Serbian Tricolour Hound (Standard No. 229)
sources.evidence: FCI documents devoted, kind, lively, dependable temperament with remarkable tenacity; scent-hound use; 1946 rejection of its former variety status and recognition as a distinct breed. Medium robust rectangular hound, deep red base with black mantle and controlled white marks, hanging ears and full low tail. FCI recognized the breed on July 25, 1961.

VBO:0201434.summary: Working Kelpies are alert, eager stock dogs bred to manage sheep in open country and in yards, then settle between jobs. Their work calls for smooth, economical movement and the judgment to solve problems as a flock shifts. The working strain is selected around ability in the field, a different emphasis from the show Kelpie's appearance standard.
VBO:0201434.shortDescription: Alert and eager around stock, this Australian working strain is valued for judgment and smooth, tireless movement.
VBO:0201434.historicalRoots: Australian working Kelpie stock-dog strain selected for sheep work across open country and yards.

sources.title: Working Kelpie Council of Australia: Characteristics and Conformation
sources.evidence: Working Kelpie Council explicitly contrasts working-strain selection with the show/ANKC standard, describes an alert, eager, friendly worker able to relax; sheep and other livestock work in open country and yards. It prioritizes sound, economical movement and describes a medium lithe dog, 10:9 body-to-height, pricked ears, low full tail and short flat coat.

sources.title: Working Kelpie Council of Australia: Origin of the Kelpie
sources.evidence: WKC history traces the working Kelpie to nineteenth-century Australian working-collie stock, describes selection for sheep work across harsh country, and says modern working Kelpies solve flock problems for themselves.

VBO:0201246.summary: Slovensky Kopovs are spirited scent hounds known for keeping their direction while following a warm trail. In Slovakia they can work a track for hours, giving tongue as they pursue wild boar. Their compact, lightly built frame supports the sustained movement this work demands.
VBO:0201246.shortDescription: Spirited and sure of direction, this Slovak hound follows a warm trail for hours and gives tongue on boar hunts.
VBO:0201246.historicalRoots: Slovak black-and-tan scent hound used to follow warm boar trails for hours while giving tongue.

sources.title: FCI: Slovenský Kopov (Standard No. 244)
sources.evidence: FCI cites hours-long following of a warm scent with voice, native use in wild boar hunting, spirited temperament and excellent direction sense. It describes a compact light but solid black-and-tan hound, rounded hanging ears and full low tail to hock.

VBO:0201275.summary: Spanish Hounds are affectionate and calm off the hunt, yet notably brave when following larger game. Hunters listen to changes in the hound's voice to tell whether it has found an old line, a fresh one or the end of a chase. The Sabueso also has a long reputation for hare work, recorded in Spanish hunting writing since the late Middle Ages.
VBO:0201275.shortDescription: Calm and affectionate off the hunt, this Spanish hound changes its voice as a scent trail develops.
VBO:0201275.historicalRoots: Sabueso Español documented in late-medieval Spanish hunting texts; specialist in hare and blood tracking.

sources.title: FCI: Spanish Hound (Standard No. 204)
sources.evidence: FCI describes an affectionate calm dog courageous on big game; hunters interpret modulations in its voice for cold/fresh scent and chase events, with hare hunting and blood tracking specialties. Historical section cites fourteenth-century hunting text. It describes white-and-orange hound, long twisted hanging ears, rectangular body and full low tail.

VBO:0200205.summary: Kind and affectionate at home, the Bourbonnais Pointing Dog becomes a passionate, adaptable hunter in varied terrain. Its head-high scent search and precise point are long-standing hallmarks of this French gundog; breeders revived the rare breed after restrictive coat and tail selection had threatened its survival.
VBO:0200205.shortDescription: Kind and affectionate at home, this French pointer hunts with a head-high scent search and a precise point.
VBO:0200205.historicalRoots: A French pointing dog from the Bourbonnais, documented by the late sixteenth century and revived by breeders in the 1970s.

sources.title: FCI No. 179
sources.evidence: Temperament describes affectionate home behavior, adaptable scent searching and pointing; history documents rarity and 1970s revival.

VBO:0200578.summary: Self-assured and attentive, double-coated German Shepherds combine a watchful manner with a willingness to follow direction. Developed from central and southern German herding dogs, the breed’s organized breeding began in 1899 with a clear aim: a capable working dog whose character mattered as much as its build.
VBO:0200578.shortDescription: Attentive and self-assured, this German herding dog was developed for working character as well as sound structure.
VBO:0200578.historicalRoots: Developed in Germany from regional herding dogs after the founding of the breed club in 1899; double coat is one FCI-recognized coat variety.

sources.title: FCI No. 166
sources.evidence: One breed character and history apply to both coat varieties; standard specifies attentive, willing character and the double coat’s close harsh guard hairs. FCI historical overview specifies methodical breeding from central/southern German herding dogs beginning in 1899 for high working ability, selecting physical constitution and character.

VBO:0200643.summary: Sociable and affectionate with people, the Griffon Fauve de Bretagne keeps a tenacious hunter’s interest in scent and difficult terrain. This old Breton hound once followed wolves; after wolf hunting faded, enthusiasts preserved the line and its short, repeated hunting voice remains part of the breed’s field character.
VBO:0200643.shortDescription: Sociable with people and tenacious on scent, this old Breton hound has a wolf-hunting past.
VBO:0200643.historicalRoots: An old Breton scent hound once used for wolf hunting; French breeders restored the line after its decline.

sources.title: FCI No. 66
sources.evidence: History documents wolf hunting and later preservation; temperament and general appearance describe sociability, affection, difficult-terrain ability and sustained voice.

VBO:0200619.summary: Docile but wilful, the Grand Griffon Vendéen is an assiduous tracker with a fine nose and resonant voice. Built for large hunting territories, it can work through thorny undergrowth while following game; the old Vendéan line carries contributions from several historic French hounds.
VBO:0200619.shortDescription: Docile yet wilful, this large Vendéan hound tracks through thorny cover with a fine nose and carrying voice.
VBO:0200619.historicalRoots: An old French Vendéen scent hound shaped by the Greffier line and other historic French hunting dogs.

sources.title: FCI No. 282
sources.evidence: History covers old Vendéan lines; behavior describes fine nose, voice, sustained tracking, thorny-cover work and docile but wilful character.

VBO:0200075.summary: Happy and sociable, the Ariégeois was shaped for active scent work rather than sheer bulk. This French hound drives game toward waiting hunters, works alone or in a pack across difficult terrain, and is known for initiative and a ringing voice; hare has been its favorite quarry.
VBO:0200075.shortDescription: Happy and sociable, this light French hound works difficult terrain with initiative and a ringing voice.
VBO:0200075.historicalRoots: Developed in France’s Ariège from a Briquet crossed with a pack hound, likely a Gascony line.

sources.title: FCI No. 20
sources.evidence: Utilization describes hare and difficult-terrain work alone or in packs; behavior describes initiative, resounding voice, sociability and trainability.

VBO:0200579.summary: Attentive and self-assured, long-coated German Shepherds share the breed’s responsive, even-tempered character. Their roots lie in central and southern German herding dogs, brought together in a deliberate breeding program for demanding work; the longer coat is one of two recognized varieties.
VBO:0200579.shortDescription: Self-assured and responsive, the long-coated German Shepherd shares a history shaped by demanding herding work.
VBO:0200579.historicalRoots: Developed from regional German herding dogs after 1899; long and harsh outer coat is a recognized variety of the same breed.

sources.title: FCI No. 166
sources.evidence: Standard applies one character and history to both coat varieties while distinguishing long outer guard hair, ear/leg tufts and bushy tail. FCI historical overview specifies methodical breeding from central/southern German herding dogs beginning in 1899 for high working ability, selecting physical constitution and character.

VBO:0201080.summary: Docile and devoted to familiar people, the Posavatz Hound is a lively Croatian scent hound with a clear, melodic hunting voice. Its stamina supported hare, fox and boar pursuits and tracking work in the Sava valley; historical depictions and records place red hounds of this type there for centuries.
VBO:0201080.shortDescription: Docile and devoted, this Croatian hound brings stamina and a clear, melodic voice to scent work.
VBO:0201080.historicalRoots: An old red-wheaten scent hound of Croatia’s Sava valley, with related hounds depicted and recorded over several centuries.

sources.title: FCI No. 154
sources.evidence: Utilization covers stamina, hare/fox/boar and tracking; temperament describes docility, devotion and melodic voice; history covers old Sava-valley records.

VBO:0201203.summary: Self-confident and driven in the field, the Segugio Maremmano was shaped by Tuscan boar hunters for work in the Maremma landscape. Its voice changes with phases of the hunt, and it can pursue quarry alone or in a pack; the breed also works hare and other mammals.
VBO:0201203.shortDescription: Self-confident in the field, this Tuscan hound uses a changing voice to mark phases of the hunt.
VBO:0201203.historicalRoots: Developed from local hunting dogs in southern Tuscany’s Maremma for wild boar work, with formal breed efforts since the 1930s.

sources.title: FCI No. 361
sources.evidence: History traces Maremma/Tuscan boar work; behavior describes drive, confidence, differentiated voice and solo or pack hunting.

VBO:0201305.summary: Tough and determined on a track, the Styrian Coarse-Haired Hound was developed for mountain hunting and wounded-game tracking. The breed traces to an 1870 cross arranged by Carl Peintinger in Styria; its rough weather-ready coat supports a hound known for giving tongue while working difficult terrain.
VBO:0201305.shortDescription: Tough and determined on mountain tracks, this Styrian hound gives tongue as it follows game.
VBO:0201305.historicalRoots: Developed in Styria from an 1870 Hanoverian Scent Hound–coarse-haired Istrian Hound cross selected for mountain work.

sources.title: FCI No. 62
sources.evidence: History documents Peintinger’s 1870 cross; utilization and temperament describe mountain tracking, determined hunting and giving tongue.
